doc.title: John Abercrombie interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 19, 2001

title: Choosing jazz, his parents, and finding Berklee
summary: At 13 or 14 he decided on jazz, with little support from parents or school; Berklee's catalogue showed him a path.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: And at what age was that kind of decision?

Early. The beginning of high school years, probably like 13, 14. And you know early teenager. And I had some friends in my town who were two brothers who played music and they would take me into their little room where they had their stash of records and they’d play me Dave Brubeck, Miles, Barney Kessel, Horace Silver, whatever. And so they were really hip and way ahead of the time. Of course then I went to my mother and told her I wanted to be a jazz musician. You have to realize I’m first generation, my parents come from England and Scotland, so I mean it would have been difficult for American parents to understand jazz or even know what it meant but for them it was like, jazz? What’s jazz? Nobody knows what jazz is. And even in my high school most people didn’t know what jazz was, and I remember the music teacher trying to discourage me from wanting to go to music school to study jazz. She says, “You don’t really want to do that, John, do something serious.” I said well, “But we like the way this sounds.” So in other words in the 50s you couldn’t get a lot of encouragement if you were a young, White kid in the suburbs, because the music wasn’t there. Nobody listened to it. And so you kind of had to like say well this is what I really want. And then I found Berklee, which was really probably one of the greatest things because Berklee was one of the only places that taught jazz and was serious about it. There were very, very few places that would even accept a guitar, even if you played classical guitar you couldn’t get in, there was no program for it. Of course here I was with my little Gretch electric guitar and my amplifier and I wanted to play music. And I opened up the Berklee catalogue and there was a picture of Gabor Szabo from Hungary, standing there with a Gretch guitar. I said I relate. I can go here, you know, this guy plays electric guitar and he’s studying at this school. And I went there and I think there were like ten guitar players the first year. Now there’s about over a thousand. Unbelievable how much it’s grown. But that was kind of how I got into playing guitar. So the 50s rock & roll was very important to me. And then I kind of naturally seemed to move into Barney Kessel, who like I say was the first one, and I still love the way he plays. But he was the first one I really heard that excited me and made me want to play the guitar.
